name: Thanaka paste

card.summary: A pale yellow paste made by grinding tree bark with water, worn on the face in Myanmar as a cooling, mattifying, sun-shielding cosmetic.
card.note: Patch-testing is customary for any new topical; laboratory data on thanaka are mostly on extracts, not people.

quick.overview:
Thanaka is a cosmetic paste from Myanmar, made by grinding the bark (and sometimes wood or root) of certain trees, chiefly Limonia acidissima, with a little water. Worn as a pale matte layer on the cheeks, it is used for a smooth, cooled, evenly toned look and as a daily sun shield.

Laboratory studies on bark extracts have found antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and mild tyrosinase-inhibiting activity, and a UV-absorbing coumarin has been proposed as the main active. No controlled trials in people on facial appearance have been reported.
quick.how: Traditionally the bark is rubbed with water on a flat stone slab to make a paste, then applied by hand or brush in circles, stripes or leaf shapes on the cheeks and nose, or across the face and arms. Ready-made powders, soaps and creams are also sold. It is typically worn through the day and washed off at night.
quick.risks: A 2010 laboratory study found no detectable genotoxicity and very low cytotoxicity in bark extracts. Reports of allergy are not prominent in the literature reviewed, but as with any plant topical, individual reactions are possible. Imported products vary in quality.

lead: Thanaka is a cosmetic paste distinctive to Myanmar, prepared by grinding the bark, wood or roots of trees such as Limonia acidissima (also called Hesperethusa crenulata) with water [1][2]. It is worn mainly by women and girls but also by men and boys, usually on the cheeks and face [2].

People use it for a matte, evenly pale finish, for the cooling feel it leaves on the skin in hot weather, and as a traditional protection against sun. Practitioners and traditional accounts also credit it with helping acne and keeping skin smooth [2][3].

Research consists mainly of laboratory work. A 2010 study of bark extracts reported anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity, mild tyrosinase inhibition (relevant to pigmentation) and slight antibacterial activity, with no detectable genotoxicity [4]. A 2024 study profiled glycerol-based extracts for antioxidant compounds [5].

paras: Thanaka is made from the bark, wood or roots of several trees; Murraya species and wood apple are named in common accounts, and regional varieties such as Shwebo and Shinmadaung are prized [2]. Traditionally the bark is ground with a little water on a slate slab with a drainage channel called a kyauk pyin, giving a creamy paste with a scent compared to sandalwood [2]. Commercial powders, soaps and creams from Myanmar brands are now sold abroad [6].

The paste is applied in circles on the cheeks, stripes, leaf shapes or over the whole face and arms [2]. It dries to a pale yellowish matte layer and is said to feel cooling [2][6]. Wearers describe it as sun protection, a complexion smoother and an acne aid [2].

A 2014 historical article states that thanaka has been used as a cosmetic by the Burmese for over 2,000 years, and that equipment once used by royalty to grind it is displayed in museums [1]. Wikipedia reports its earliest literary mentions in a 14th-century poem and 15th-century works [2]. Myanmar has reportedly nominated thanaka culture for UNESCO intangible heritage listing [6].

No human trials of thanaka on facial appearance were found. A 1998 field study on the Thai-Myanmar border tested deet and permethrin repellents mixed with thanaka among Karen women; the repellent combination gave strong protection against mosquitoes and pregnant women preferred versions mixed with thanaka as a base [7]. Laboratory studies are described below.

A 2010 study tested bark extracts and found strong anti-inflammatory, significant antioxidant, mild tyrosinase-inhibiting and slight antibacterial activity, and no detectable genotoxicity; the authors concluded that watery paste use is safe [4]. Coumarins such as marmesin are suggested to be the UV-absorbing agents [2][6]. A 2024 study found glycerol extracted more bioactive compounds than ethanol or water [5].
